foundations.heading: The Foundations
foundations.subtitle: Strong fundamentals for reliable, accessible software.

html.title: Semantic HTML
html.description: Every site is built from semantic HTML5 elements, with proper landmark roles (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <article>, <section>). That gives the page a logical document structure: something search engines can read and assistive technologies can move through efficiently. SEO and accessibility both benefit from the same work.

css.title: Modern CSS
css.description: CSS Grid and Flexbox for responsive layouts, container queries for component-level responsiveness, and custom properties (design tokens) for theming that stays maintainable. No bloated CSS frameworks. Modern CSS is powerful enough on its own, and dropping the legacy libraries means smaller bundles and faster page loads.

typescript.title: JavaScript & TypeScript
typescript.description: TypeScript brings type safety to JavaScript, catching bugs at compile time instead of runtime. Strongly typed interfaces define the data contracts and autocomplete speeds up the writing, but the bigger win is that refactoring stops being a gamble. Fewer errors reach production, and whoever maintains the code next gets up to speed faster.

frameworks.heading: Frameworks and Tooling
frameworks.subtitle: Vue 3, Nuxt, and Vite for high-performance modern applications.

vue.title: Vue 3
vue.description: Vue 3 is a progressive JavaScript framework for building user interfaces. The Composition API makes logic reusable and testable, and it works properly with TypeScript. The reactivity system is efficient and predictable, and single-file components (.vue files) keep template, logic and styles together in one place. Add the small bundle size and the performance that comes with it, and Vue suits marketing sites and complex applications equally well.

SSR hands fully-rendered HTML to search engines and users on the first request, which helps SEO and perceived performance. SSG pre-renders pages at build time, so they can be served at maximum speed from an edge cache. File-based routing cuts out the boilerplate and makes the codebase easier to work in.

apis.heading: APIs and Integrations
apis.subtitle: Secure, versioned, and well-documented API design.
apis.p1: Plenty of applications need a backend API to handle data, authentication, payments and third-party integrations. We design and build REST and GraphQL APIs with clear OpenAPI contracts, semantic versioning and proper documentation. REST endpoints follow standard HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error) and use HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) consistently.
apis.p2: Authentication uses established protocols: OAuth 2.0 for delegated access and JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for stateless session management. Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse, and CORS policies are configured correctly for cross-origin requests. Backend services are built in .NET (C#) or Node.js depending on what the project needs, both strongly typed and both with mature frameworks behind them.
apis.p3: Data persistence uses relational databases (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL) with normalised schema design, appropriate indexing, and transactional integrity. Third-party integrations include payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal), booking systems (Booksy, Square), CRM platforms (HubSpot, Zoho), and email services (Mailchimp, SendGrid). Each integration is abstracted behind a clean interface so dependencies can be swapped without rewriting application logic.
apis.p4: REST and GraphQL solve the same problem differently. REST gives you one URL per resource and is simpler to cache, debug and document, which makes it the right default for most business websites and integrations. GraphQL gives the client a single endpoint and lets it ask for exactly the fields it needs. That earns its keep when one screen pulls from many sources, or when mobile bandwidth is a real constraint, and it costs you more complex caching and a steeper learning curve. For a small business site with a contact form and a booking integration, REST is almost always the correct answer, and we will say so rather than sell you complexity you do not need.

accessibility.heading: Accessibility Built In From the Start
accessibility.subtitle: WCAG 2.2 compliance for inclusive, usable web experiences.
accessibility.p1: Every site we build targets WCAG 2.2 Level AA. That is the standard referenced by UK accessibility obligations and the level most commercial and public sector contracts ask for, and it covers the success criteria that matter most in practice: keyboard operability, screen reader support, colour contrast and error handling. Accessibility is designed in from the first decision rather than retrofitted before launch, because retrofitting is where the cost lands. WAI-ARIA attributes (aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-live, role) are used sparingly and correctly, to add semantics where HTML alone falls short rather than to patch over markup that should have been semantic in the first place.
accessibility.p2: Keyboard operability gets tested properly: every interactive element has a visible focus indicator, focus order follows reading order, and keyboard traps are removed. Screen reader testing is done with NVDA (Windows) and VoiceOver (macOS/iOS), checking that announcements are clear, that landmarks can be navigated and that dynamic content updates are communicated through live regions. Colour contrast meets or exceeds WCAG AA ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text), and colour is never the only thing carrying information. For users who prefer reduced motion, the prefers-reduced-motion media query serves alternative animations or static layouts.
accessibility.p3: Forms are built for clarity and error recovery. Labels are properly associated with inputs, validation errors are announced to screen readers and linked via aria-describedby, and error messages tell the user what to do about it. There is a legal side too: accessible websites are required under the UK Equality Act 2010 for businesses providing services to the public, and public sector bodies must meet the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018. The commercial case is simpler. More people can use the site, everyone finds it easier to use, and search engines reward well-structured, semantic markup.
accessibility.p4: WCAG 2.2, published in October 2023, adds nine success criteria on top of WCAG 2.1 rather than replacing it, so a site that meets 2.2 Level AA also meets 2.1 Level AA. The additions mostly concern focus visibility and appearance, dragging alternatives, target size (a minimum 24 by 24 CSS pixels for interactive controls), consistent help placement, and reducing the cognitive load of authentication and redundant data entry. If a contract or tender asks you to meet "WCAG 2.1 AA", building to 2.2 satisfies it with room to spare.

gdpr.heading: UK GDPR and Data Protection
gdpr.subtitle: Privacy-first design and compliance with UK data protection law.
gdpr.p1: Every project is designed for UK GDPR compliance from the outset. Personal data processing rests on a lawful basis (consent, contractual necessity, legitimate interests, legal obligation), documented clearly in the privacy policy. Data minimisation means collecting only what is necessary. Purpose limitation keeps that data to the stated purpose, and storage limitation sets the retention period after which it is securely deleted. Consent for analytics and marketing cookies is obtained explicitly through opt-in banners under PECR (Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations), and a user can withdraw that consent at any time, which triggers immediate deletion of tracking cookies.
gdpr.p2: Analytics configurations respect privacy. Google Analytics 4 is set up with IP anonymisation enabled, sensitive data kept out of event parameters, and data retention periods set appropriately. Where a privacy-focused alternative fits the project, we will recommend it. Data subject rights under UK GDPR (access through subject access requests, rectification, erasure or the right to be forgotten, data portability, and objection) are supported through clear processes and the technical implementation to back them. The ICO (Information Commissioner's Office) publishes the regulatory guidance, and we help clients work out what it means for them as data controllers.
gdpr.p3: Data in transit is encrypted using TLS 1.2 or higher (HTTPS everywhere), and sensitive data at rest is encrypted using industry-standard algorithms (AES-256). Where data is hosted, we prefer UK or EU data residency to avoid the complications of international transfers, which is straightforward on Microsoft Azure using the UK South or UK West regions. Backups are encrypted and tested regularly, and disaster recovery procedures are written against defined recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO).
gdpr.disclaimer: This information is provided for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice. Consult a qualified data protection solicitor for specific legal requirements.

cloud.heading: Cloud-First Hosting
cloud.subtitle: Microsoft Azure and edge-optimised infrastructure.
cloud.p1: Modern hosting is cloud-first. Microsoft Azure provides scalable, reliable infrastructure with global edge delivery through Azure Static Web Apps, Azure App Service and Azure CDN. Static sites are deployed to Azure's edge network and served from the closest point of presence (PoP) to the user, which keeps latency down. TLS/HTTPS is on by default, with certificates renewed automatically through Let's Encrypt or Azure-managed certificates, so connections stay encrypted and browsers show the trust indicators visitors look for.
cloud.p2: Environments are kept separate (development, staging, production) using Azure resource groups and deployment slots, so changes can be tested safely before they reach production. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic spikes without anyone intervening. Uptime is monitored with Azure Monitor and Application Insights, with alerting configured for performance degradation, errors or downtime. Costs stay under control through resource tagging, budget alerts and right-sizing of compute and storage. Cloud infrastructure does not need to be expensive, particularly for a small business with predictable traffic patterns.
cloud.p3: Infrastructure as code (IaC) is used where it earns its place, defining resources declaratively in Bicep or Terraform templates so deployments are reproducible and infrastructure changes are version-controlled. Backups run automatically and are tested to confirm the restore procedure works, and rollback mechanisms are in place if a problem shows up after release. Azure's UK regions (UK South, UK West) keep data inside UK borders, which simplifies GDPR compliance and meets organisational data residency requirements.

containers.heading: Containerisation and CI/CD
containers.subtitle: Docker and automated pipelines for reliable deployments.
containers.p1: Docker containers package an application and its dependencies into a reproducible, portable image that runs the same way in development, staging and production. That is the end of 'works on our machine'. Dockerfiles define multi-stage builds: the compile and test stages throw away everything that is not needed, and only the final runtime image, holding the compiled application and its production dependencies, gets deployed. Smaller image, smaller attack surface.
containers.p2: Container images are pushed to a container registry (Azure Container Registry, Docker Hub) with semantic versioning tags, so a failed deployment can be rolled back to a previous version. Base images are kept up to date with security patches, and vulnerability scanning tools (Trivy, Snyk, Azure Defender) pick up known CVEs in dependencies. Image layers are cached with some thought: dependency installation is cached separately from application code, so dependency downloads are skipped when package manifests haven't changed.
containers.p3: CI/CD pipelines automate delivery through clearly defined stages. Lint checks enforce code style, type checks verify TypeScript correctness, unit and integration tests validate behaviour, builds produce optimised bundles, and deployments push to the target environment. Automated preview deployments spin up ephemeral environments for pull requests, so stakeholders can review changes before anything is merged to main. If a deployment introduces a bug, automated rollback policies revert to the last known good version and the downtime stays short.

performance.heading: Performance and Core Web Vitals
performance.subtitle: Fast, measurable user experiences that drive conversions.
performance.p1: Performance is not a matter of opinion. It is measured, using Google's Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance and should occur within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness to user input and should be below 200ms, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability and should be below 0.1. Those numbers feed user experience, conversion rates and Google search rankings, so we optimise every project to meet or beat the Good thresholds.
performance.p2: Images are delivered in modern formats (AVIF with WebP fallback) and sized per viewport using responsive image syntax (srcset and sizes attributes). Lazy loading holds offscreen images back until the user scrolls near them, which cuts the initial page weight. Fonts use font-display: swap to avoid invisible text (FOIT), subset down to the character ranges you need. Critical CSS is inlined in the document head so above-the-fold content renders immediately, and the rest is loaded asynchronously.
performance.p3: JavaScript bundles are code-split by route, so a visitor only downloads the code for the pages they open. Third-party scripts (analytics, chat widgets) are loaded asynchronously or deferred so they do not block the main thread. Caching headers are set aggressively for static assets: immutable files are cached for one year with cache-busting hashes in the filenames, and stale-while-revalidate serves the cached copy instantly while fetching an update in the background. Pages end up feeling fast to use, and that shows up in the conversion figures.

seo.heading: Technical SEO
seo.subtitle: Technical SEO and answer-engine optimisation, built in from the start.
seo.p1: Technical SEO is what lets search engines crawl, index and rank your content. Semantic HTML structure with a correct heading hierarchy (one h1 per page, logical h2-h6 nesting) tells them what matters and how it relates. Metadata covers title tags (55-60 characters), meta descriptions (150-160 characters) and Open Graph tags for rich social media previews. JSON-LD structured data (Schema.org markup) adds explicit semantic context: LocalBusiness, Product, Article, BreadcrumbList and FAQPage schemas help search engines identify content types and show rich results in SERPs.
seo.p2: Sitemaps (XML and HTML) list all pages for crawlers, and robots.txt files control crawler access to specific paths. Canonical URLs (rel=canonical) prevent duplicate content penalties, and 301 redirects guide search engines when URLs change. Server-side rendering (SSR) delivers fully-rendered HTML to crawlers on first request, which is what makes JavaScript-heavy applications indexable. Client-side rendering leaves the crawler to execute the JavaScript itself, and not all of them do that reliably. Nuxt's SSR mode handles it.
seo.p3: Internationalisation (i18n) with hreflang tags signals language and regional variants to search engines, which heads off duplicate content problems on multilingual sites. This site is bilingual, English and Welsh, with the hreflang annotations done properly. Performance work (fast LCP, low CLS) feeds SEO rankings directly through Google page experience signals. Regular audits using Lighthouse, Search Console and Screaming Frog turn up technical problems (broken links, missing alt text, slow pages) and track how rankings move over time.

staticSites.heading: What a Static Site Is, and Why It Matters to You
staticSites.subtitle: The delivery model behind fast, cheap-to-run, hard-to-break websites.
staticSites.p1: A static site is one where every page is built into finished HTML ahead of time, at the moment the site is published, rather than assembled by a server each time somebody visits. The visitor's browser is handed a complete page immediately. There is no database query, no server-side rendering step, and no waiting.
staticSites.p2: In practice that means three things for a business. It is fast, because the page is already made, and that feeds straight into Core Web Vitals and therefore search ranking. It is cheap to run: serving files costs a fraction of running an application server. And breaking in is hard when there is no database to compromise, no admin login exposed to the internet and no plugin ecosystem to keep patched.
staticSites.p3: The trade-off is that anything properly dynamic (live stock levels, a customer account area, a booking calendar showing real availability) still needs a service behind it. So most of our builds are static pages with specific dynamic pieces called in as needed, rather than an all-or-nothing choice. This website is built exactly that way: every page in both English and Welsh is prerendered at build time.

builders.heading: Website Builders vs a Custom Build
builders.subtitle: An honest comparison of Wix, Squarespace, WordPress and a bespoke site.
builders.p1: Website builders are good at what they do. Wix plans run from around £9 to £119 a month and Squarespace from around £12 to £79 a month, both with templates, hosting and a visual editor included. If you need something online this week, you are comfortable doing it yourself, and the site is a simple shopfront, a builder is a reasonable answer and we will tell you so.
builders.p2: The costs show up later. Subscriptions do not stop, and they rise. Templates constrain what you can do, so the site ends up looking like every other business using that template. Performance and accessibility are largely out of your hands, and both feed search ranking. Apps and add-ons are billed separately, often £5 to £30 a month each. And the site is not portable: you cannot take a Wix site to another host, so what you have is a rental.
builders.p3: WordPress sits in between: flexible and portable, but it is an application that needs maintaining. Core, theme and plugin updates have to be applied, and unpatched plugins are the single most common route into a small business website. Either you do that work monthly or you pay somebody to.
builders.p4: A custom build costs more up front and takes longer. What you get for it is a site nobody else has, built to accessibility and performance standards you can point at, with no subscription attached to the site itself and full ownership of the code and accounts. For a business where the website is a real sales channel rather than a formality, that usually pays back. If you just need a placeholder online by Friday, it does not, and a builder is the honest recommendation.

milestones.heading: How Milestones Work
milestones.subtitle: Regular check-ins so you know where the project stands.

item1.title: Milestone Reviews
item1.description: Each milestone ends with a demo of working software, a written note covering what changed and what's next, and a budget check against the plan.

item2.title: What You Can See

item3.title: Adapt or Stop
item3.description: Priorities change and budgets tighten. At any milestone boundary we can re-scope or stop work, so you are not tied to a contract that no longer fits.

ai.heading: AI-Assisted and Agentic Delivery
ai.subtitle: Modern tooling to deliver more value for your budget.

item1.title: AI Tooling Throughout
item1.description: AI-assisted coding tools help with scaffolding, boilerplate generation, test creation, refactoring, documentation and code review assistance. This speeds up repetitive work without sacrificing quality.

item2.title: Agentic Workflows
item2.description: Agentic workflows handle multi-step tasks like schema migrations, bulk refactors, generating TypeScript types from API specs, and scaffolding i18n translations. Work that would previously burn billable hours is automated, freeing budget for design decisions and testing.

item3.title: More Value, Less Typing
item3.description: More of your budget goes into requirements refinement, user experience design and testing, and less into typing boilerplate that a machine can write faster and more accurately.

item4.title: Human Accountability and Review
item4.description: Every line of code is reviewed by a human before it ships. Nothing is merged without passing automated checks (linting, type checking, tests, accessibility scans) and manual code review. The developer remains accountable for the output, whatever tool produced the first draft.

item5.title: Data Privacy and Guardrails
item5.description: AI tooling does not have access to client production data, secrets, API keys, or sensitive business logic. Confidentiality and GDPR obligations govern what can and cannot be shared with third-party services. If your project has strict data handling requirements, AI tooling is restricted or disabled accordingly.

quality.heading: Quality Gates
quality.subtitle: Seven automated and manual checks every project passes before it goes live.

item1.title: Code Review
item1.description: Every change is reviewed before merge. Code quality, logic correctness, test coverage and security implications are checked manually.

item2.title: Automated Tests
item2.description: Unit tests validate individual functions and components. End-to-end tests simulate real user journeys through the application. Tests run on every commit.

item3.title: Type Checking
item3.description: TypeScript catches type errors, null reference bugs and interface mismatches at compile time, which removes a whole class of runtime errors.

item4.title: Accessibility Checks
item4.description: Automated accessibility scans check for WCAG 2.2 Level AA violations: missing alt text, insufficient contrast, keyboard traps, unlabelled form fields. Manual testing with screen readers validates real usability.

item5.title: Performance Budgets
item5.description: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) are measured on every build. Budgets are set for bundle size, image weight and request counts. Performance regressions are caught before they reach production.

item6.title: Dependency Scanning
item6.description: Automated vulnerability scanning checks for known CVEs in dependencies. Security updates are applied promptly and tested before deployment.

item7.title: Staging Sign-Off
item7.description: Nothing goes to production without sign-off on staging. You see and approve the working software before it launches.

hosting.heading: Hosting and Environments
hosting.subtitle: Cloud-first infrastructure with automated deployments and rollback.
hosting.p1: Hosting is cloud-first on Microsoft Azure with separate development, staging and production environments. Containerised builds using Docker keep them consistent, so what works in development works in production. Infrastructure as code (Bicep or Terraform) defines resources declaratively, making deployments reproducible and version-controlled.
hosting.p2: CI/CD pipelines automate the build and deployment process: code is linted, type-checked and tested automatically; builds produce optimised production bundles; deployments push to staging first for review, then production after approval. Rollback is built in. If a deployment introduces a regression, the previous version is restored within minutes.
hosting.p3: Monitoring and logging track application health, error rates and performance metrics. Alerts notify on downtime, slow responses or a spike in errors. Automated backups run daily with retention policies, and restore procedures are tested to confirm they work. Releases end up predictable and low-drama, with problems caught early and fixed fast.

working.heading: Working Together
working.subtitle: What you can expect from us, and what we will need from you.
working.p1: We are UK-based and work UK business hours (Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm GMT/BST). You have one named point of contact, the person building the site, not an account manager relaying messages. Communication happens on an agreed channel (email, Slack, Teams, or phone) with an agreed cadence for check-ins. Updates are written in plain English, and we will tell you when something turns out harder or cheaper than we first thought.
working.p2: You own your code, your domain and your hosting accounts from day one. There are no lock-in clauses, no proprietary platforms, and no ongoing fees required to keep your site running beyond standard hosting and domain costs. If you want to take the project in-house or to another developer, everything transfers with documentation and support during handover.
working.p3: We will agree deadlines we think are achievable, and say so when priorities conflict. Holidays and illness are flagged in advance, with a plan for anything urgent in the meantime. When your requirements change, we work out the impact on cost and timeline before committing to new work. And if a deadline or a budget starts to look at risk, you hear about it as soon as we know rather than at the next scheduled check-in.

faq.heading: Common Questions
faq.subtitle: Straight answers to the questions we get asked most about how projects run.

q1.question: What if my requirements change mid-project?
q1.answer: Requirements change on most projects. At each milestone boundary, we can re-prioritise the backlog or adjust scope. If a change is significant, we assess the impact on cost and timeline and present options before proceeding. A fixed scope agreed at the start does not bind you once the business need has moved on.

q2.question: How do I know progress is real and not just a status update?
q2.answer: Every milestone delivers working software on a staging URL that you can click through and test. Progress notes include links to the staging environment and describe what was built, what changed, and what is next. You see the actual application evolving, not a Gantt chart or a percentage-complete figure.

q3.question: Can we start small and expand later?
q3.answer: Yes. For larger projects, we propose phasing options where the first phase delivers a working minimum viable product (MVP) or a specific high-value feature set. You launch with something useful and proven, then expand in later phases as budget allows and business priorities become clearer. This reduces risk and allows early feedback from real users.

q4.question: Who owns the code and the accounts?
q4.answer: You do. Source code is stored in a Git repository that you own (GitHub, GitLab, Azure Repos). Hosting accounts, domain registrations, and third-party service accounts (analytics, payment gateways) are created in your name or transferred to you at handover. There are no lock-in clauses or proprietary platforms. If you decide to take the project elsewhere, it all goes with you.

q5.question: What happens after launch?
q5.answer: Support after launch is optional. We offer ongoing maintenance retainers covering bug fixes, dependency updates, content changes, and small feature additions. Alternatively, you can handle maintenance in-house or engage another developer. The codebase is documented, and we run a handover session so whoever takes it on can pick it up without guessing. Nothing about the build requires you to keep paying us.

q6.question: How is AI used, and is my data safe?
q6.answer: AI tools assist with scaffolding, boilerplate, refactoring, test generation and documentation. Every line is reviewed by a human and tested before shipping. AI does not have access to production data, secrets, API keys, or sensitive client information. If your project has strict data handling requirements, AI tooling is restricted or disabled. GDPR and confidentiality obligations decide what can be shared with a third-party service at all.

q7.question: How long does it take to build a small business website?
q7.answer: Most small business sites launch 2 to 6 weeks after first contact. That breaks down as 1 to 2 days of discovery, 2 to 3 days to produce the proposal, 2 to 5 days refining requirements, 1 to 3 weeks of build in weekly milestones, and 2 to 4 days for launch and handover. The single biggest variable is how quickly you can get us your content: photos, service descriptions, opening hours. Projects that stall almost always stall there.

q8.question: Should I use a small studio or a large agency?
q8.answer: A large agency gives you depth of bench: designers, copywriters, project managers and developers under one roof, which matters on a big multi-team build. You pay for that structure, and you usually talk to an account manager rather than the person doing the work. A small studio like ours gives you a direct line to the developers, lower overheads in the quote, and faster decisions, at the cost of that bench depth. For a small business website, an online shop or a booking system, the agency structure is overhead you are paying for and rarely using.

cost.p1: Enquiries go to a competitor who is easier to find. Customers shortlist businesses they can verify online before picking up the phone. If you do not have a website, you are not on that shortlist.
cost.p2: Being passed over looks like a quiet spell or a seasonal dip, when often it is invisibility. You lose work to businesses that present better online, even when your work is better than theirs. And the same questions keep eating into your day when a page could answer them once.

faq.heading: Straight Answers
faq.subtitle: Common questions from small business owners.

q1.question: I'm not technical. Will I be able to manage it?
q1.answer: Yes. The site is built to run without you needing to touch code. Contact form submissions come to your email. If you want to update text or add a new photo later, a simple content management interface can be included, or changes can be requested and handled for a small fee. A walkthrough session at handover shows you everything.

q2.question: Do I need to write all the content myself?
q2.answer: You know your business best, so the core content (what you do, where you serve, your prices or approach) needs to come from you. But templates and example text are provided to make it easier. If you are stuck, a content workshop can be included to pull the right words out of a conversation and turn them into clear web copy.

q3.question: What if I already have a domain or a half-finished site?
q3.answer: Existing domains can be transferred or pointed to the new site without losing your email or existing setup. Half-finished sites can be replaced cleanly or, if the foundation is sound, improved and completed. Each situation is different, so this is discussed during the initial conversation.

q4.question: Will it work on phones?
q4.answer: Yes. Every site is designed mobile-first, which means it is built for phones and tablets before desktops. Most visitors to a small business site are on a phone, so that is where the design starts.

q5.question: Do I need a cookie banner and privacy policy?
q5.answer: Yes, if you use analytics or any tracking. UK GDPR and PECR require explicit consent before setting non-essential cookies, and you must tell users what data you collect and why. A compliant cookie banner and privacy policy are included as standard, written in plain English and linked in the footer.

q6.question: Can it grow later if my business grows?
q6.answer: Yes. Small business sites are built with clean, maintainable code on modern infrastructure. Adding a booking system, an online shop, a blog or extra service pages later is straightforward. The setup does not box you in as the business grows.

q7.question: What happens if I want changes after it's live?
q7.answer: Minor fixes within the first month are included. After that, small changes (text updates, new photos, an extra page) can be handled on a pay-as-you-go basis or as part of an optional monthly maintenance retainer. You own the site and can take it elsewhere whenever you like.

bespoke.forWho: These vary far too much in scope to price fairly with a published figure. A ten-product shop and a two-hundred-product shop are different jobs. Tell us what you need and you get a clear, itemised quote with no obligation.

care.heading: Keeping It Running
care.subtitle: Optional. You own the site either way.
care.p1: Hosting, security patching, dependency updates, automated backups, uptime monitoring and small content changes: opening hours, prices, a new service, a batch of photos. It stops the site quietly rotting after launch.
care.p2: If you would rather handle it yourself or hand it to another developer, that is fine. The code is documented, the accounts are in your name, and there is no exit fee.

bilingual.heading: Welsh Language Sites
bilingual.p1: A full bilingual English and Welsh version of any package adds roughly 30 to 40 per cent, depending on how much content needs translating. That covers separate URLs for each language, correct hreflang annotations, proper language tagging and a working language switcher, rather than a translation widget bolted on top. This website is built that way, so you can see the result before you commit.

ownership.heading: What You Own
ownership.p1: The domain is registered in your name, not ours, and so are the hosting account and the source code. You pay the registrar directly, usually £10 to £15 a year, which means the domain is yours to keep and yours to take with you if you ever move to another developer. Third-party fees, such as Stripe's transaction charges, are also paid by you directly and sit outside the prices above.

pricing.faqSubtitle: The things people ask before they commit to a number.
pricing.q1: Why publish prices when most web designers do not?
pricing.a1: Because the alternative wastes everybody's time. If our starting price is well above your budget you should be able to find that out in ten seconds rather than after two phone calls, and if it is comfortably within your budget you should be able to see that before you get in touch. Hidden pricing usually means the price depends on how much the buyer looks like they can afford. Ours does not.
pricing.q2: Is a cheaper website a worse website?
pricing.a2: Not automatically, but you should know what you are buying. A £300 site is usually a template with your logo dropped in, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to buy if that is what you need. What you usually do not get is accessibility standards, Core Web Vitals tuning, or the ability to move it to another host. Ask any quote what happens if you want to move it elsewhere in two years.
pricing.q3: How does this compare to Wix or Squarespace?
pricing.a3: Builders cost less up front and more over time. Wix runs roughly £9 to £119 a month and Squarespace roughly £12 to £79, forever, plus apps billed separately, and you cannot take the site with you if you leave. A Starter site at £650 with no compulsory monthly fee breaks even against a mid-tier builder subscription in around two to three years, and you own it outright. If you need something online this week and you are happy to build it yourself, a builder is the better answer, and we will say so.
pricing.q4: Do I have to pay it all up front?
pricing.a4: No. Payment is split across the milestones in the proposal: typically a deposit to start, a payment at an agreed midpoint, and the balance on launch. It is all set out in writing before anything begins.
pricing.q5: What if my project grows halfway through?
pricing.a5: Change is normal. At each milestone boundary we can re-prioritise or adjust scope, and anything that affects cost or timeline is shown to you as options before it is agreed, not invoiced as a surprise afterwards.
pricing.ctaBody: Tell us what you are trying to do and you will get a straight answer about scope, cost and timescale. No obligation and no sales pressure.

ecommerce.kicker: eCommerce Website Design: Cardiff, Swansea, Newport and South Wales
ecommerce.title: Online Shops That Are Yours to Keep
ecommerce.subtitle: A proper online shop with secure payments, real stock control and no monthly platform fee attached to the site itself.

intro.p1: We build online shops for independent retailers across South Wales, from a single-product store to a full catalogue with variants, stock levels and delivery zones. Payments run through Stripe or PayPal, so card data never touches your site and you are not liable for storing it.
intro.p2: The important difference from a hosted platform is ownership. A Shopify or Wix shop is rented: the subscription never ends, the apps are billed separately, and you cannot move the shop elsewhere. What we build is yours (the code, the domain, the hosting account) and there is no compulsory monthly fee for the site to keep existing.
intro.p3: That trade-off is not right for everyone. If you are selling a handful of items and want to be live this week, a hosted platform is the better answer and we will tell you so. Custom pays back when the shop is a real sales channel, when it has to look like nobody else's, or when it needs to talk to the stock and accounting systems you already run.

The variables are catalogue size, how many product options each item has, what has to integrate with your stock or accounts, and whether product photography and descriptions need writing. You get a fixed written quote before any work starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Online Shops
faq.subtitle: What retailers ask us before committing.

q1.question: Is a custom shop cheaper than Shopify or Wix in the long run?
q1.answer: It depends how long you run it and how many add-ons you need. A hosted platform costs roughly £20 to £100 a month once you include apps, for as long as you trade. A custom shop costs more up front and then only hosting, which for a static-fronted shop is a few pounds a month. Most shops break even somewhere in years two to four. If you expect to trade for a season, rent. Own it if this is the business.

q2.question: Can I manage products myself without touching code?
q2.answer: Yes. You get an admin area for adding and editing products, prices, stock levels and images. If your catalogue already lives somewhere else (a spreadsheet, an EPOS system, an accounting package), we can often import from it or sync with it instead of asking you to retype everything.

q3.question: How are card payments kept secure?
q3.answer: Card details are entered directly into Stripe or PayPal's own hosted checkout, so they never pass through or get stored on your site. That keeps you out of scope for the strictest parts of PCI DSS compliance. Your site only ever sees whether a payment succeeded and what was ordered.

q4.question: Will my products show up in Google Shopping?
q4.answer: We add Product structured data to every item: price, availability, images, description. That is what Google reads to build a shopping result. It makes eligibility possible without guaranteeing placement, and paid Shopping campaigns are a separate thing we do not run for you.

q5.question: What about postage, VAT and returns?
q5.answer: Postage rules, delivery zones and collection options are set up as part of the build, so a Cardiff customer and a customer in Inverness can be charged differently. VAT is handled correctly on invoices. Returns policy wording is yours to decide, but we will make sure it is published where UK consumer law requires it to be.

booking.kicker: Online Booking Systems: Bridgend, Cardiff, Swansea and South Wales
booking.title: Stop Losing Bookings to Voicemail
booking.subtitle: Let customers book themselves in, day or night, without you answering the phone mid-appointment.

intro.p1: Most missed bookings have nothing to do with a competitor's better prices. They are lost because somebody rang while you had your hands full, did not leave a message, and booked with whoever answered next. An online booking system takes that call for you at eleven at night, on a Sunday, and while you are with a client.
intro.p2: We build booking into your own website rather than sending customers off to a third-party marketplace. Two reasons for that. The booking belongs to you rather than being a lead rented from a platform that also advertises your competitors. And the customer stays on your site, with your prices, photos and reviews in front of them.
intro.p3: Where you already use Booksy, Square or something similar and it works, we integrate rather than replace. Your site becomes the front door and the existing system stays the diary. If there is no system, or the one you have does not fit how you work, we build one that does.

included.f6: Cancellation and rescheduling rules you set, enforced automatically

whoFor.heading: Who Buys This

whoFor.item4Description: Fitness instructors, tutors and workshop hosts selling places in a session rather than one-to-one appointments, with capacity limits and waiting lists.

pricing.heading: What a Booking System Costs
pricing.body: A website with booking or payment integration starts at £1,250 and typically takes 2 to 3 weeks of build time. That covers a working booking flow wired into your calendar, with confirmations and reminders. More complex setups (multiple staff, deposits, class capacity, syncing with an existing system) are quoted on top, in writing, before work starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Booking Systems
faq.subtitle: What salons and trades ask us before committing.

q1.question: I already use Booksy. Do I have to move?
q1.answer: No. If Booksy works for you, keep it. We integrate with it so your website shows real availability and hands the booking over cleanly. Moving only makes sense if you are paying for something you have outgrown, or if the platform's own marketing is pushing your customers towards competitors.

q2.question: Will it stop people booking when I'm closed or already busy?
q2.answer: Yes. Availability comes from your actual calendar, with your opening hours, buffer times, holidays and existing appointments all respected. Double-booking is prevented at the point of booking rather than discovered afterwards.

q3.question: Can I take a deposit to cut down no-shows?
q3.answer: Yes, through Stripe: either a fixed deposit or the full amount at the point of booking, and you choose which services require it. Combined with automatic reminder emails, that is the most effective no-show reduction available. Your cancellation and refund terms are yours to set and we implement them.

q4.question: What happens if a customer wants to change or cancel?
q4.answer: They get a link in their confirmation email that lets them reschedule or cancel within the window you set, say more than 24 hours ahead. Outside that window it tells them to contact you instead. That keeps the easy changes off your phone without letting somebody cancel a Saturday slot at nine on Saturday morning.

q5.question: Do I need a whole new website to get booking?
q5.answer: Not necessarily. Booking can often be added to an existing site if it is in reasonable shape and you own it. On a platform you cannot modify, or a site that is slow and hard to find in search, you will usually get more out of rebuilding. The booking work is the same either way.

businessWebsite.kicker: Business Website Design: Bridgend, Cardiff, Swansea and South Wales
businessWebsite.title: A Website That Does the Explaining For You
businessWebsite.subtitle: For businesses that do not sell online and do not take bookings, but do need to be found, understood and trusted.

intro.p1: Plenty of businesses do not need a shop or a booking diary. They need a site that turns up when somebody searches, answers the questions they get asked on every first call, and looks like it belongs to a firm worth hiring. That is a smaller job than an online shop and it should cost less.
intro.p2: The work is mostly in structure and clarity. One page per service, so each can rank for what people search for. A roofer needs separate pages for flat roofs, repairs and emergency callouts rather than one page listing all three. Clear contact details on every page. Enough detail that a prospect can qualify themselves before they ring you, so the calls you do get are better ones.
intro.p3: This is also where the professional-credibility argument lives. If somebody is about to hand you a serious brief, they will look you up first. A site that loads fast, reads well and works properly on a phone is doing quiet work in that moment, and a slow one built in 2014 is doing the opposite.

included.f2: Location and service-area content for the towns you cover
included.f3: Contact details and a working enquiry form reachable from every page
included.f4: Photo galleries of finished work, optimised so they do not slow the site
included.f5: LocalBusiness structured data feeding Google's local results
included.f6: WCAG 2.2 Level AA accessibility and Core Web Vitals performance targets

whoFor.heading: Who Buys This
whoFor.subtitle: Businesses whose website is a credential, not a till.
whoFor.item1Description: Accountants, solicitors, surveyors and independent consultants, where the site has to stand up to being checked before somebody commits to a serious piece of work.
whoFor.item2Description: Builders, roofers and electricians who lose search traffic by cramming every service onto one page instead of giving each its own.
whoFor.item3Description: Businesses whose site was fine a decade ago and is now slow, unreadable on a phone, and quietly costing them the enquiries they never hear about.
whoFor.item4Description: Charities, clubs and community organisations that need clear public information, accessible to everyone, without a budget for an agency.

pricing.heading: What a Business Website Costs
pricing.body: A straightforward business website starts at £650 for up to five pages, typically 1 to 2 weeks of build time once we have your content. More pages, more service-specific landing pages, or content that needs writing rather than supplying will lift that, and you get the exact figure in a written quote before anything starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Business Websites
faq.subtitle: What firms ask us before committing.

q1.question: How many pages do I actually need?
q1.answer: Usually one per thing you want to be found for, plus the basics. A plumber offering boiler repairs, bathroom installation and emergency callouts needs three service pages. Search engines match a search to a page, so more focused pages means more chances to be found. Five pages covers most small firms; ten is common once each service gets its own.

q2.question: Do I have to write all the content myself?
q2.answer: No, but supplying the raw material speeds things up and keeps the cost down. Most small business sites need 500 to 1,000 words in total. Give us rough notes, a list of services and some photos and we can shape it from there. If you would rather we wrote it from an interview, that is quoted as extra.

q3.question: What if I already have a domain or a half-finished site?
q3.answer: That is normal and usually fine. We can take over an existing domain without any downtime, and an unfinished site is often still useful for its content and photos even if the build itself is not worth keeping. You keep ownership of the domain throughout.

q4.question: Can it grow later if the business grows?
q4.answer: Yes. Adding pages, a blog, booking or a shop later is normal. Because you own the code and it is built on standard technology rather than a proprietary platform, expanding it does not mean starting again. It does not have to be us that does it, either.

q5.question: Will it work properly on phones?
q5.answer: Yes, and that is where most of your visitors will be. Every site is designed mobile-first and built to pass Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds, which measure loading, responsiveness and visual stability on real devices rather than on a developer's fast desktop.

bespoke.kicker: Bespoke Software Development: South Wales and Remote
bespoke.title: When Off-the-Shelf Software Nearly Fits
bespoke.subtitle: Client portals, internal tools, dashboards and workflow systems, built around the way your business runs.

intro.p1: Most businesses reach a point where the software is shaping the process rather than serving it. The signs are familiar: a spreadsheet nobody is allowed to touch, the same information typed into three systems, a monthly report that takes somebody two days, or a subscription paid for one feature out of forty.
intro.p2: We design and build custom web applications for that gap: client portals, booking and scheduling systems, internal dashboards, quoting tools, and integrations that make existing systems talk to each other. Built on .NET or Node with a typed front end, hosted on Microsoft Azure, with the same accessibility and security standards as everything else we ship.
intro.p3: We are also happy to tell you when not to build. If a £30-a-month product does ninety per cent of what you need, buying it is the right answer and we will say so. Custom is worth it when the remaining ten per cent is where your margin lives, when nothing off the shelf fits the workflow, or when the licence cost across your team has outgrown the cost of owning the thing outright.

included.f6: Authentication, role-based permissions and audit trails where needed

included.f8: Source code in your own repository from day one, with no lock-in

whoFor.heading: Who Buys This
whoFor.subtitle: The problems that justify building rather than buying.
whoFor.item1Description: Firms whose clients need somewhere to see their own documents, jobs, invoices or progress without emailing to ask.
whoFor.item2Description: Businesses running on a fragile spreadsheet that has become load-bearing, where one wrong paste breaks a week.
whoFor.item3Description: Organisations retyping the same data into a booking system, an accounts package and a CRM because none of them talk to each other.
whoFor.item4Description: Businesses whose software is the thing they sell, needing a technical partner to build or extend it properly rather than quickly.

pricing.heading: What Bespoke Software Costs
pricing.body: Bespoke work is quoted individually. There is no honest range to publish, because scope varies more than in any other kind of project. The same three-word description can mean two weeks or six months. What you get instead is a free discovery conversation, a straight view on whether building is even the right call, and a fixed written quote with assumptions and exclusions stated plainly before any work begins.

faq.heading: Questions About Bespoke Software
faq.subtitle: What businesses ask before commissioning a build.

q1.question: How do I know custom is the right answer?
q1.answer: Usually it is not, and we will tell you. Buy off the shelf when a product covers the need at a sensible licence cost. Build when nothing fits the workflow, when the workaround is costing real hours every week, when the data has to move between systems that will not talk, or when per-seat licensing across a growing team has passed what owning it would cost. Discovery exists to answer that question before you spend anything.

q2.question: Can we start small instead of committing to everything?
q2.answer: Yes, and for most projects that is what we recommend. The first phase delivers a useful slice of the thing (one workflow, one user group) that you can put in front of real users. What they do with it usually changes what phase two should be, and finding that out early is much cheaper than building the whole thing first.

q3.question: What happens if we want to take it elsewhere?
q3.answer: Everything transfers. Source code lives in a repository you own from day one, hosting and third-party accounts are in your name, and handover includes documentation and a walkthrough. There are no proprietary platforms and no clauses making it awkward to leave.

q4.question: Is AI used in the build, and is our data safe?
q4.answer: AI tools assist with scaffolding, boilerplate, refactoring, test generation and documentation, and every line is reviewed by a human and tested before it ships. AI tooling is not given access to production data, secrets, API keys or client information. If your project has specific data handling requirements, say so at discovery and they go into the written scope.

q5.question: What about support after launch?
q5.answer: Support is optional, and we will talk it through openly. It can be a maintenance retainer covering fixes, dependency updates and small changes, or a clean handover to your own team or another developer. The codebase is documented either way, so keeping your software running does not depend on us.
